title: Mineral and Energy Resources
seo_title: Year 12 Earth and Environmental Science: Mineral and Energy Resources Worksheets
standard_code: Earth and Environmental Science Unit 3: Use of non-renewable Earth resources
standard_text: How mineral and energy resources form (magmatic, hydrothermal, sedimentary and residual deposits, coal, oil and gas); ore and ore grade; exploration and mining methods; Australian resources; reserves and the lifetime of non-renewable resources. (Senior Secondary Earth and Environmental Science, Unit 3: Living on Earth – extracting, using and managing Earth resources)
meta_desc: Free Year 12 Earth and Environmental Science worksheets on mineral and energy resources: ores, ore grade, exploration, mining, coal, oil, gas, uranium, lithium and Australian deposits. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Ore = a deposit that can be mined at a profit.
key_sub: Mass of metal = mass of ore × grade.
body_html:
How to think about it

Minerals become concentrated by geological processes: crystallisation of magma, hot (hydrothermal) fluids, weathering (bauxite), sedimentation (banded iron, placer gold) and burial of organic matter (coal, oil and gas). Whether a deposit is ore depends on its grade, size, depth and the price of the metal.

Deposits are found by geological mapping, geophysics and drilling, then mined by open-cut or underground methods. Australia is a world leader in iron ore, coal, LNG, gold, bauxite, uranium and lithium. Non-renewable reserves last only as long as reserves ÷ rate of use.

Example

5000 t of ore at 1.2% copper. Copper?

5000 × 1.2 ÷ 100

Answer: 60 t

Example

Reserves 600 Mt, use 20 Mt per year. Lifetime?

600 ÷ 20

Answer: 30 years

Common mistakes

  • Calling any metal-bearing rock an ore.
  • Forgetting to divide the percentage by 100.
  • Thinking fossil fuels form in a human lifetime.

faq.q: Why does Western Australia have so much iron ore?
faq.a: Banded iron formations laid down 2.5 billion years ago in the Hamersley Basin were later enriched by weathering to very high-grade ore.

faq.q: Why are reserves estimates always changing?
faq.a: New discoveries, better technology and changing prices change how much of a deposit can be mined profitably.

items.q: How does bauxite form?
c: intense weathering in a hot, wet climate leaches other minerals and leaves aluminium oxides
items.e: It is a residual deposit.

items.q: What is uranium used for in energy production?
c: as fuel for nuclear fission reactors
as a fuel in coal power stations
items.e: Australia has the world's largest uranium reserves but no nuclear power stations.

items.q: William asks how iron ore formed. What is the best explanation?
c: from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers
from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries
from rain and snowmelt soaking into porous rock and sediment (aquifers)
from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years
items.e: Iron ore formed from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers.

items.q: Lachlan reads about a resource that formed from rain and snowmelt soaking into porous rock and sediment (aquifers). Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how groundwater formed.

items.q: How did the rock of Wave Rock in Western Australia form?
c: from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented
items.e: Wave Rock in Western Australia is granite (igneous).

items.q: What kind of rock is Kata Tjuta made of?
items.e: It formed from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together.

items.q: What is liquefied natural gas (LNG)?
c: natural gas cooled to about −162 °C so it becomes a liquid for transport
items.e: Australia is one of the largest LNG exporters.

items.q: How did black coal in the Bowen and Sydney Basins form?
c: plant material from ancient swamps was buried and changed by heat and pressure over millions of years
items.e: Most is Permian, about 250–300 million years old.

items.q: How did the rock of Uluru form?
c: from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented
from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from layers of river sand pressed together
from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
items.e: Uluru is arkose, a sandstone (sedimentary).

items.q: When is open-cut mining used rather than underground mining?
c: when the ore is very deep and narrow
when the ore is large and close to the surface
items.e: The Super Pit at Kalgoorlie is open-cut.

items.q: How did the rock of Sydney's harbour cliffs form?
c: from layers of river sand pressed together
from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented
from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
items.e: Sydney's harbour cliffs is Hawkesbury sandstone (sedimentary).

items.q: Why is lithium important for the energy transition?
c: it is a fuel for jet engines
it is used in rechargeable batteries for electric vehicles and storage
it replaces coal in steel making
items.e: Western Australia is a major lithium producer.

items.q: What is the purpose of drilling core samples in exploration?
c: to find the depth, size and grade of a possible ore body
items.e: Assays of the core give the grade.

items.q: Mei reads about a resource that formed from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how coal formed.

items.q: How did the rock of Kata Tjuta form?
c: from rounded pebbles and boulders cemented together
from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented
from layers of river sand pressed together
from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
items.e: Kata Tjuta is conglomerate (sedimentary).

items.q: Tom asks how coal formed. What is the best explanation?
c: from seawater evaporating in shallow basins long ago
from rain and snowmelt soaking into porous rock and sediment (aquifers)
from hot, mineral-rich water and magma near volcanoes and plate boundaries
from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years
items.e: Coal formed from plants from ancient swamps buried and squeezed for millions of years.

items.q: Where are Australia's largest iron ore mines?
c: the Hunter Valley, New South Wales
the Pilbara region of Western Australia
items.e: The ore formed from banded iron formations.

items.q: Which Australian deposit is one of the world's largest of copper, gold and uranium?
items.e: It is mined underground.

items.q: What is an ore?
c: a pure metal found in nature
rock containing a mineral in high enough concentration to be mined at a profit
items.e: Whether a deposit is ore depends on price and cost.

items.q: Noah reads about a resource that formed from iron that settled out of ancient oceans in layers. Which resource is it?
items.e: That is how iron ore formed.

items.q: A deposit holds 4000 million tonnes. Production is 50 million tonnes a year, but a new mine will raise it by 2%. Using the higher rate, about how long will the deposit last?
items.e: New rate = 50 × 1.02 = 51 Mt per year; 4000 ÷ 51 = 78.4 years.

items.q: How did the gold of the Kalgoorlie 'Golden Mile' form?
c: hot fluids carried dissolved gold through fractures and deposited it in quartz veins
items.e: These are hydrothermal deposits.

items.q: A coal deposit has reserves of 300 million tonnes. If 10 million tonnes are mined each year, how long will the reserves last?
items.e: Lifetime = reserves ÷ rate = 300 ÷ 10 = 30 years.

items.q: What is a placer deposit?
c: heavy minerals such as gold concentrated by flowing water in river or beach sands
items.e: The 1850s Victorian gold rush was mostly placer gold.

items.q: A deposit holds 4000 million tonnes. Production is 80 million tonnes a year, but a new mine will raise it by 2%. Using the higher rate, about how long will the deposit last?
items.e: New rate = 80 × 1.02 = 81.6 Mt per year; 4000 ÷ 81.6 = 49 years.

items.q: How do oil and natural gas form?
c: remains of marine plankton are buried, heated and changed into hydrocarbons, which collect in traps
items.e: They need a source rock, reservoir rock and cap rock.

items.q: What is mineral processing (beneficiation)?
c: crushing ore and separating the valuable mineral from the waste rock
items.e: Flotation separates many sulfide minerals.

items.e: Drilling then confirms the ore.

items.q: Where is bauxite (aluminium ore) mined in Australia?
c: Weipa (Queensland) and the Darling Range (Western Australia)
items.e: Bauxite forms by deep tropical weathering.

items.q: Why can a deposit that was not ore become ore?
c: a rise in metal price or a cheaper mining method makes it profitable
the deposit moves closer to the surface
the metal grows in the rock
items.e: Economics defines ore.

items.q: What is ore grade?
c: the concentration of the valuable mineral or metal in the ore
items.e: Gold is measured in grams per tonne; iron as a percentage.

items.q: Zara learns that an aquifer holds 800 billion litres. People pump out 20 billion litres a year, and rain refills only a small amount. About how many years until it runs low (ignoring refill)?
items.e: 800 ÷ 20 = 40 years. Pumping faster than refilling depletes groundwater.
